title: Working with Both Syntaxes knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which mental model best explains “Working with Both Syntaxes” in Dart Sass?
options: Readable SCSS guarantees correct browser rendering, accessibility, and performance without output review.
The best solution is always to replace native CSS behavior with a new Sass abstraction.

Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax.
The browser executes Sass source directly, so a compilation step is unnecessary.
questions.answer_key: Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax.
questions.explanation: Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax. The alternative choices confuse Sass compilation with browser execution or claim guarantees that require independent tests.

questions.prompt: When applying “Reading SCSS code”, which approach is the most reliable?
options: Silence every warning before determining whether it identifies a deprecated or incorrect construct.
For reading scss code, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.
Skip compilation and infer the final selector list and property values from the source file alone.
Prefer deeply nested selectors because fewer source lines always mean simpler and safer CSS.
questions.answer_key: For reading scss code, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.
questions.explanation: For reading scss code, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation. Compare the compiled output with the stated intent and preserve browser-native behavior where it is required.

questions.prompt: Which review decision most directly supports maintainability for “Working with Both Syntaxes”?
options: Start with a small example, state the expected CSS behavior, compile it with Dart Sass, and compare the output with the intent. Retain the plain-CSS alternative when Sass adds no meaningful reuse or organization.
Generate every possible selector or theme combination, even when most variants are never used.
Treat successful compilation as proof that the interface is accessible and behaves correctly in every browser.
Expose internal implementation details as public API and postpone documentation until after release.
questions.answer_key: Start with a small example, state the expected CSS behavior, compile it with Dart Sass, and compare the output with the intent. Retain the plain-CSS alternative when Sass adds no meaningful reuse or organization.
questions.explanation: Start with a small example, state the expected CSS behavior, compile it with Dart Sass, and compare the output with the intent. Retain the plain-CSS alternative when Sass adds no meaningful reuse or organization. The other choices increase output, assume unverified behavior, or make the public interface harder to maintain.
